pageTitle: Recording Microphones: Transducer Physics, Polar Patterns & Studio Capture
subtitle: Master dynamic moving-coil, condenser electrostatic, and ribbon velocity mechanics, polar pattern mathematics, and stereo arrays

introduction.title: The Microphone: Acoustic Energy Transduced into Electrical Voltage
introduction.text: Every microphone is a precision acoustic transducer operating at the front line of music production. Its physical mechanism determines how air pressure fluctuations—ranging from the delicate flutter of a nylon-string guitar to the violent sound pressure of a cranked tube amplifier—are transformed into microvolt electrical signals. The choice of microphone is never an arbitrary tonal filter: moving-coil dynamics bring mechanical mass and transient smoothing; electrostatic condensers deliver lightning-fast rise times and crystalline overtone resolution; and corrugated aluminum ribbons harness acoustic particle velocity to deliver smooth, unhyped analog warmth. Understanding the transducer physics and polar pattern mathematics is the foundational skill of the recording engineer.
introduction.quote: A microphone does not just capture sound; its diaphragm mass and acoustic polar geometry define what the listener experiences as space, distance, and intimacy.

columns.title: Transducer Physics & Diaphragm Mass
columns.text: The transient response of any microphone is strictly governed by Newton's second law: F = m · a. A dynamic microphone diaphragm carries a copper wire voice coil glued to its rear, giving it substantial physical mass and inertia. Consequently, it naturally smooths over harsh, spiky transients and withstands immense sound pressure levels exceeding 150 dB SPL. Conversely, a studio condenser diaphragm consists of a micro-thin gold-sputtered Mylar membrane (often only 3 to 5 microns thick) operating without an attached coil. Its near-zero inertia reacts almost instantaneously to ultrasonic frequencies, yielding extraordinary transient fidelity.

columns.title: Polar Pattern Mathematics & Phase Geometry
columns.text: How a microphone hears off-axis sound is a function of acoustic delay and pressure differential. A pure pressure transducer (omnidirectional) seals the rear of the diaphragm, responding purely to atmospheric pressure changes with zero proximity effect. A pressure-gradient transducer exposes both sides of the diaphragm to sound. By combining pressure and pressure-gradient ports in precise acoustic ratios, engineers create the cardioid family (E = (1 - k) + k \cosθ), allowing selective rejection of room reflections and adjacent instruments.

cards.title: Dynamic Moving-Coil Microphones
cards.description: The nearly indestructible workhorses of modern studios and concert stages worldwide.

fields.label: Transduction Principle
fields.value: Electromagnetic induction (Faraday's Law). Diaphragm motion moves an attached copper coil through a permanent magnetic field, generating audio voltage without external power.

fields.label: SPL Handling
fields.value: Virtually immune to internal distortion; handles massive volumes up to 150–160 dB SPL (snare drums, cranked 4x12 guitar cabinets, brass).

fields.label: Frequency & Transient Profile
fields.value: Controlled high-frequency rolloff above 15 kHz with a sculpted presence peak between 3 kHz and 7 kHz that pushes vocals and snares forward in a mix.

fields.label: Best Applications
fields.value: Close-miking guitar amps, snare top, kick drum (inside), rock vocals, live broadcast

cards.title: Electrostatic Condenser Microphones
cards.description: Ultra-sensitive, high-fidelity transducers capturing breath, air, and delicate harmonic detail.

fields.label: Transduction Principle
fields.value: Variable electrostatic capacitance (Δ C = \epsilon A / d). A gold-sputtered Mylar diaphragm sits microns away from a fixed brass backplate, polarized by +48V phantom power.

fields.label: Transient Rise Time
fields.value: Micro-second transient recovery capturing the strike of acoustic guitar picks, room reverberation tails, and vocal breath nuances.

fields.label: Large vs Small Diaphragm
fields.value: Large Diaphragm Condensers (LDC ≥ 1") provide lower self-noise and warm low-frequency proximity bloom; Small Diaphragm Condensers (SDC ≤ 0.5") offer ruler-flat frequency linearity and superior off-axis coherence.

fields.label: Best Applications
fields.value: Lead vocals, acoustic guitars, drum overheads, grand piano, orchestral strings

cards.title: Ribbon Velocity Microphones
cards.description: Vintage acoustic warmth and velvety high-end response prized by purists and modern producers alike.

fields.label: Transduction Principle
fields.value: Particle velocity sensing. An ultra-thin (1.5 to 2.5 micron) corrugated pure aluminum ribbon is suspended between powerful neodymium magnets.

fields.label: Tonal Profile
fields.value: Naturally smooth, gradual high-frequency rolloff that completely eliminates the harsh 'digital sizzle' of bright cymbals, distorted guitars, and aggressive horns.

fields.label: Polar Characteristic
fields.value: Inherent bi-directional (Figure-8) pattern with infinite acoustic nulls at 90° and 270° sides for surgical acoustic isolation.

fields.label: Handling Warning
fields.value: The corrugated ribbon can be stretched or torn by direct gusts of air or accidental DC phantom power on vintage transformerless designs. Always use a pop filter.

cards.title: Polar Pattern Architecture
cards.description: Polar patterns define the three-dimensional directional sensitivity of the microphone capsule.

fields.label: Cardioid (1 + \cosθ)
fields.value: Maximum sensitivity at 0° (front); -6 dB at 90°/270° sides; infinite null at 180° (rear). The primary choice for isolating a performer from untreated room reflections and stage monitor feedback.

fields.label: Supercardioid & Hypercardioid
fields.value: Narrower front pickup angle than cardioid with sharper side rejection nulls at 120° (supercardioid) or 110° (hypercardioid), at the expense of a small rear sensitivity lobe.

fields.label: Omnidirectional (Pure Pressure)
fields.value: Equal sensitivity from all 360° directions. Exhibits zero proximity effect, ruler-flat bass extension down to 10 Hz, and extreme resistance to breath plosives.

fields.label: Figure-8 (Bidirectional)
fields.value: Equal sensitivity front (0°) and rear (180°), with total phase cancellation and acoustic silence at the 90° and 270° sides. Indispensable for stereo arrays.

cards.title: The Physics of the Proximity Effect
cards.description: The proximity effect is the dramatic boost in low-frequency response that occurs when a sound source approaches a directional microphone.

fields.label: The Physical Cause
fields.value: In directional (pressure-gradient) microphones, sound reaches both sides of the diaphragm. At close distances (< 6 inches), the inverse-square law creates a massive pressure difference between front and rear ports at low frequencies, boosting bass by up to +12 dB below 150 Hz.

fields.label: Creative Vocal Power
fields.value: Broadcasters and vocalists use proximity effect intentionally to add authoritative, chesty radio warmth and intimate fullness to quiet vocal deliveries.

fields.label: Combating Mud
fields.value: When close-miking guitar amps, kick drums, or backing vocalists, engage the microphone's built-in 80 Hz high-pass filter (HPF) to eliminate uncontrolled low-end buildup.

cards.title: Shure SM57
cards.description: The undisputed king of instrument recording, found on every professional drum kit, guitar cabinet, and concert stage on earth.

fields.label: Type & Pattern
fields.value: Dynamic moving-coil, Cardioid

fields.label: Frequency Response
fields.value: 40 Hz to 15,000 Hz with sculpted presence peak at 5 kHz–7 kHz

fields.label: SPL Handling
fields.value: >150 dB SPL without breakup

fields.label: Signature Sound
fields.value: Punchy midrange bite that lets electric guitar cabs and snare drums slice through dense mixes

cards.title: Shure SM7B
cards.description: The legendary large-diaphragm dynamic vocal microphone immortalized on Michael Jackson's Thriller and trusted as the global podcasting gold standard.

fields.label: Type & Pattern
fields.value: Dynamic moving-coil with internal air suspension, Cardioid

fields.label: Shielding & Rejection
fields.value: Electromagnetic humbucking coil rejects broadband interference from computer monitors and power lines

fields.label: Output Sensitivity
fields.value: Low output (-59 dBV/Pa); requires a high-gain preamp (60 dB+) or Cloudlifter inline booster

fields.label: Tone Profile
fields.value: Velvety, smooth, unhyped vocal authority with Bass Rolloff and Mid-Range Boost switches

cards.title: Coincident (XY) vs Near-Coincident (ORTF)
cards.description: Capturing a realistic acoustic stereophonic soundstage requires careful management of time and intensity cues.

fields.label: Coincident XY Pair
fields.value: Two identical directional capsules placed at the same physical point in space, angled 90° to 120° apart. Relies purely on intensity differences between channels with zero time delay (Δ t = 0), guaranteeing 100% phase-perfect mono summing.

fields.label: ORTF System
fields.value: Developed by French broadcasting. Two cardioid capsules angled 110° apart with capsules spaced 17 cm (6.7 inches) apart—replicating the distance between human ears. Combines timing and intensity differences to deliver natural spatial width and holographic depth.

fields.label: Blumlein Pair
fields.value: Two Figure-8 microphones crossed at 90° with capsules stacked vertically. Captures a 360° stereo picture with authentic lateral room ambience, ideal for balanced acoustic ensembles.

cards.title: Mid-Side (M/S) Matrixing & The 3:1 Rule
cards.description: Advanced stereo configurations that prevent destructive comb-filtering.

fields.label: Mid-Side (M/S) Architecture
fields.value: A forward-facing cardioid (Mid) captures the center image, while a sideways-facing figure-8 (Side) captures stereo width. Decoded via phase splitting: Left = Mid + Side; Right = Mid - Side.

fields.label: Monophonic Safety
fields.value: When collapsed to mono, the positive and negative side signals cancel completely (+S + (-S) = 0), leaving the pristine Mid signal completely unaffected by phase comb-filtering.

fields.label: The 3:1 Distance Rule
fields.value: When using multiple microphones on an instrument or ensemble, the distance between any two microphones should be at least three times the distance from each microphone to its intended sound source (D_mic-to-mic ≥ 3 · D_mic-to-source) to avoid audible comb filtering.
